track.title: Corporate Finance
track.tagline: One concept, term and calculation at a time

lessons.title: Time value of money
lessons.summary: ₹100 today is worth more than ₹100 next year.

term.meaning: What money invested today grows to: FV = PV × (1 + r)^n.

sections.b: Money can earn a return, so receiving it earlier is better. Compounding means you earn returns on past returns. This idea sits under every valuation, loan and investment decision.
Companies compare projects, price loans and value businesses using the time value of money. Individuals use it for SIPs, FDs and retirement planning.

lessons.example: An FD of ₹1,00,000 at 7% for 2 years grows to ₹1,14,490: interest is earned on the first year's interest too.

calc.problem: You invest ₹10,000 at 8% per year compounded annually for 3 years. What is the future value?

quiz.q: Why is money today worth more than the same amount later?
options: It can be invested to earn a return
quiz.why: Earning capacity (and inflation) make earlier money more valuable.

quiz.q: FV of ₹1,000 at 10% for 2 years is…

lessons.title: Present value and discounting
lessons.summary: Bring future money back to today's value.

term.meaning: The rate used to convert future cash into today's value; reflects risk and opportunity cost.

sections.b: Present value reverses compounding: PV = FV / (1 + r)^n. The higher the discount rate or the longer the wait, the lower the present value.
Valuing bonds, projects and companies means discounting expected future cash flows to today.

lessons.example: A customer offers ₹1,10,000 in one year instead of ₹1,00,000 now. At a 12% discount rate, PV = ₹98,214, so take the ₹1,00,000 now.

calc.problem: What is the present value of ₹50,000 received in 4 years if the discount rate is 10%?

quiz.q: If the discount rate increases, the present value of a future cash flow…
quiz.why: A higher rate divides by a bigger number.

quiz.q: PV of ₹1,100 received in 1 year at 10% is…

lessons.title: Simple vs compound interest
lessons.summary: Compounding is interest on interest. Over time the gap is huge.

term.meaning: Earning returns on both the original amount and previously earned returns.

sections.b: Simple interest = P × r × n (interest only on principal). Compound amount = P × (1 + r)^n. The longer the period and the higher the rate, the bigger the compounding advantage.
Loans, deposits and investment returns are usually compounded. Understanding it helps you evaluate debt costs and long-term investing.

lessons.example: Rule of 72: money doubles in roughly 72 / rate years. At 12%, about 6 years.

calc.problem: Invest ₹1,00,000 at 10% for 5 years. Compare total interest under simple vs compound interest.

quiz.q: Using the Rule of 72, at 8% money doubles in about…
Simple interest on ₹10,000 at 8% for 3 years is…

lessons.title: The income statement
lessons.summary: Revenue minus costs, step by step, down to net profit.

term.meaning: Earnings Before Interest and Taxes, i.e. operating profit.

sections.b: Revenue − Cost of goods sold (COGS) = Gross profit. Gross profit − Operating expenses = EBIT. EBIT − Interest = EBT (profit before tax). EBT − Tax = Net income (PAT).
The income statement (P&L) shows profitability over a period. Each line tells a different story: pricing power (gross), efficiency (operating), financing (interest).

lessons.example: A café sells ₹10 lakh of coffee; beans and milk cost ₹4 lakh (COGS); rent and salaries ₹4 lakh. Operating profit is ₹2 lakh.

calc.problem: Revenue ₹10,00,000; COGS ₹6,00,000; Operating expenses ₹2,00,000; Interest ₹50,000; Tax rate 25%. Find net income.

lessons.title: The balance sheet
lessons.summary: What a company owns, owes and what belongs to shareholders.

term.meaning: Owners' claim on the business: Assets − Liabilities.

sections.b: The accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Assets: cash, receivables, inventory, machinery. Liabilities: loans, payables. Equity: share capital + retained earnings. It is a snapshot at a point in time.
The balance sheet shows financial strength, leverage and liquidity, which is key for lenders and investors.

lessons.example: You buy a ₹50 lakh flat with a ₹40 lakh loan. Asset ₹50L = Liability ₹40L + Your equity ₹10L.

calc.problem: A company has total assets of ₹500 crore and total liabilities of ₹320 crore. What is shareholders' equity?

quiz.why: A loan is an amount owed.

quiz.q: The balance sheet shows a position…

lessons.title: Cash flow vs profit
lessons.summary: Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact.

term.meaning: Cash generated from core business operations in a period.

sections.b: Accrual accounting records revenue when earned, not when cash arrives. The cash flow statement has three parts: operating, investing and financing. Indirect method: start with net income, add back non-cash expenses (depreciation), adjust for working capital changes.
Profitable companies can still go bankrupt if cash runs out. Lenders and investors watch operating cash flow closely.

lessons.example: A company books a ₹10 lakh sale on 90-day credit: profit rises today, but cash comes only in 3 months.

calc.problem: Net income ₹100; Depreciation ₹30; Receivables increased by ₹40; Payables increased by ₹10. Calculate operating cash flow (₹ lakh).

quiz.why: Sales not yet collected tie up cash.

quiz.q: Raising a bank loan appears in…

lessons.title: Working capital
lessons.summary: The cash needed to run day-to-day operations.

term.meaning: Current assets − Current liabilities.

sections.b: Current assets (cash, receivables, inventory) convert to cash within a year; current liabilities (payables, short-term debt) are due within a year. Positive working capital means short-term obligations are covered.
Too little working capital risks a liquidity crunch; too much ties up cash that could be invested.

lessons.example: A retailer stocks up before Diwali: inventory rises, so working capital needs rise, often financed by a short-term loan.

calc.problem: Current assets ₹800 lakh; Current liabilities ₹500 lakh. Find net working capital and the current ratio.
steps: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities

options: Tie up cash that could be invested

lessons.title: Depreciation
lessons.summary: Spreading the cost of an asset over its useful life.

term.meaning: Estimated value of an asset at the end of its useful life.

sections.b: Straight-line depreciation = (Cost − Salvage value) / Useful life. Depreciation is a non-cash expense: it reduces profit (and tax) but not cash directly.
It matches costs with the revenue an asset helps generate and creates a tax shield.

lessons.example: A delivery van costing ₹10 lakh used for 5 years with no salvage value is depreciated at ₹2 lakh per year.

calc.problem: A machine costs ₹5,00,000, has a salvage value of ₹50,000 and a life of 5 years. Find annual straight-line depreciation.

quiz.why: Cash was spent when the asset was bought.

quiz.q: Depreciation creates a tax shield because it…

lessons.title: Break-even analysis
lessons.summary: How many units must you sell to cover all costs?

term.meaning: Selling price − Variable cost per unit; what each unit contributes to fixed costs and profit.

sections.b: Fixed costs (rent, salaries) don't change with volume; variable costs (materials) do. Break-even units = Fixed costs / Contribution margin per unit.
Used for pricing, launching products, and understanding business risk.

lessons.example: A startup with ₹3 lakh monthly fixed costs selling a ₹1,000 product with ₹400 variable cost needs 500 sales a month to break even.

calc.problem: Fixed costs ₹2,00,000; Price ₹500; Variable cost ₹300 per unit. Find break-even units and revenue.

quiz.q: If variable cost per unit rises, the break-even point…
quiz.why: Lower contribution per unit means more units needed.

lessons.title: Profit margins
lessons.summary: How much of each rupee of sales becomes profit.

term.meaning: Net income / Revenue: profit kept per rupee of sales.

sections.b: Gross margin = Gross profit / Revenue (pricing & production efficiency). Operating margin = EBIT / Revenue. Net margin = Net income / Revenue (after everything).
Margins allow comparison across companies of different sizes and track efficiency over time.

lessons.example: Software firms often have 70%+ gross margins; supermarkets often under 25%. Different business models, different margins.

calc.problem: Revenue ₹2,000 crore; Gross profit ₹800 crore; Net income ₹150 crore. Find gross and net margins.

quiz.why: Revenue minus COGS, relative to revenue.

lessons.title: EBITDA
lessons.summary: A popular measure of operating cash earnings.

term.meaning: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortisation.

sections.b: EBITDA = Net income + Taxes + Interest + Depreciation & Amortisation (or EBIT + D&A). It removes financing, tax and accounting choices to compare operating performance.
Used in valuation multiples (EV/EBITDA) and loan covenants. But it ignores capex and working capital, so it is not the same as cash.

lessons.example: Telecom companies have huge depreciation; EBITDA helps compare their operating performance before those charges.

calc.problem: Net income ₹120 cr; Tax ₹40 cr; Interest ₹30 cr; D&A ₹50 cr. Find EBIT and EBITDA.

quiz.q: A key limitation of EBITDA is that it ignores…
quiz.why: Capex is a real cash need that EBITDA leaves out.

lessons.title: CAGR: compound growth rate
lessons.summary: Smooth, annualised growth between two points.

term.meaning: Compound Annual Growth Rate = (End / Start)^(1/n) − 1.

sections.b: CAGR gives the constant yearly rate that would take a value from start to end. It hides volatility but makes comparisons easy.
Used to describe revenue growth, investment returns and market size.

lessons.example: A mutual fund going from ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh in 6 years has a CAGR of about 12.2%.

calc.problem: Revenue grew from ₹50 crore to ₹80 crore in 4 years. What is the CAGR?

quiz.q: A value tripling in 10 years has a CAGR of about…

lessons.title: Current vs non-current assets
lessons.summary: Sort what a company owns by how quickly it turns into cash.

term.meaning: An asset expected to be converted to cash or used up within 12 months.

sections.b: Current assets: cash, receivables, inventory, short-term investments. Non-current (fixed) assets: land, buildings, machinery, long-term investments, intangibles like software and brands. The split shows liquidity and capital intensity.
Lenders look at current assets to judge short-term safety; investors look at non-current assets to understand how capital-heavy the business is.

lessons.example: A steel plant is dominated by non-current assets (furnaces, land), while a software company's assets are mostly cash and receivables.

calc.problem: Cash ₹50 lakh, receivables ₹80 lakh, inventory ₹70 lakh, machinery ₹300 lakh, land ₹200 lakh. Find current, non-current and total assets.
calc.answer: Current ₹200 L; non-current ₹500 L; total ₹700 L

quiz.why: Inventory is sold within a year.

quiz.q: A capital-intensive business has a high share of…

lessons.title: Debt vs equity financing
lessons.summary: Two ways to fund a business, each with different costs and risks.

term.meaning: Total debt ÷ shareholders' equity; shows how much borrowing is used relative to owners' money.

sections.b: Debt: borrowed money with fixed interest and repayment; lenders don't own the company. Equity: owners' money; no fixed payment, but shareholders share profits and control. Debt is cheaper (tax-deductible interest) but riskier if cash flows fall.
The financing mix affects risk, control, cost of capital and how much growth the company can fund.

lessons.example: A family business may prefer a bank loan to keep control; a startup raises equity because it lacks steady cash flow to service debt.

calc.problem: A company raises ₹100 crore: ₹60 crore through a loan and ₹40 crore from shareholders. What is its debt-to-equity ratio?

quiz.why: The tax shield makes debt cheaper.

quiz.q: Why might a founder prefer debt?

options: From profits/dividends and share value growth

lessons.title: Accrual vs cash accounting
lessons.summary: When is revenue recorded: when earned, or when cash arrives?

term.meaning: Recording revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of cash timing.

sections.b: Cash accounting records transactions only when cash moves. Accrual accounting matches revenue and expenses to the period they relate to. Companies in India report under accrual-based Ind AS or Indian GAAP.
Accrual accounts show true performance; cash accounts show liquidity. You need both views to manage a business.

lessons.example: A consultant finishes a ₹5 lakh project in March but gets paid in May. Accrual: March revenue. Cash: May inflow.

calc.problem: In March a firm sells goods worth ₹10 lakh. It collects ₹6 lakh in March and ₹4 lakh in April. What is March revenue under accrual vs cash accounting?
steps: Accrual: revenue earned in March = ₹10 lakh
Cash: cash received in March = ₹6 lakh
The ₹4 lakh is a receivable at month-end
calc.answer: Accrual ₹10 L; cash ₹6 L (₹4 L receivable)

quiz.q: Under accrual accounting, revenue is recorded when…
Which basis do listed Indian companies use?

lessons.title: Revenue recognition and deferred revenue
lessons.summary: Cash received in advance isn't revenue until you deliver.

term.meaning: Cash received for goods or services not yet delivered; a liability until earned.

sections.b: Under Ind AS 115 / IFRS 15, revenue is recognised when control of goods or services passes to the customer. Subscription businesses recognise revenue over the service period.
Correct recognition prevents overstated profits. Deferred revenue also signals future revenue visibility, which investors like.

lessons.example: Netflix-style annual subscriptions: you pay upfront, but the company recognises one-twelfth each month.

calc.problem: A SaaS company receives ₹12 lakh upfront on 1 January for a 12-month subscription. How much revenue is recognised by 31 March, and what deferred revenue remains?

quiz.q: The standard for revenue recognition in India is…

lessons.title: Fixed and variable costs
lessons.summary: Which costs move with volume, and which don't?

term.meaning: A cost that changes in proportion to output, like raw materials or delivery charges.

sections.b: Fixed costs (rent, salaries, insurance) stay the same within a range of output. Variable costs rise with each unit. Total cost = Fixed + Variable per unit × Units. Average cost falls as volume rises because fixed costs are spread.
Pricing, scaling decisions and break-even analysis all depend on understanding cost behaviour.

lessons.example: A cloud kitchen pays fixed rent of ₹1 lakh a month; each meal costs ₹50 in ingredients and packaging.

calc.problem: Fixed costs ₹1,00,000 per month; variable cost ₹50 per unit; 3,000 units produced. Find total cost and average cost per unit.

quiz.q: Which is usually a fixed cost?
As output rises, average cost per unit usually…

lessons.title: Contribution margin ratio
lessons.summary: What share of each sale is left to cover fixed costs and profit?

term.meaning: (Price − Variable cost) ÷ Price; contribution per rupee of sales.

sections.b: Contribution margin per unit = Price − Variable cost. CM ratio = CM ÷ Price. Total contribution = Sales × CM ratio. Profit = Contribution − Fixed costs.
CM ratio tells you how profitable extra sales are, which helps with pricing, discounts and product-mix decisions.

lessons.example: If a discount cuts the CM ratio from 40% to 30%, you need a third more sales just to earn the same contribution.

calc.problem: Price ₹200 per unit; variable cost ₹120. Sales are ₹10 lakh. Find the CM ratio and total contribution.

options: 40 paise per rupee of sales covers fixed costs and profit

quiz.q: A discount that lowers the CM ratio means you need…
options: More sales to earn the same contribution

lessons.title: Budgets and variance
lessons.summary: Plan the numbers, then explain the gaps.

term.meaning: Difference between actual and budgeted figures; favourable or unfavourable.

sections.b: A budget is a financial plan for a period. Variance = Actual − Budget. For costs, spending more than budget is unfavourable; for revenue, earning more is favourable. Analysts explain material variances (e.g. >5-10%).
Variance analysis turns numbers into management action: why did costs rise, and what will we do?

lessons.example: Marketing spent ₹12 lakh against a ₹10 lakh budget because of an extra festive campaign: an unfavourable ₹2 lakh variance with a clear reason.

calc.problem: Travel budget ₹5,00,000; actual spend ₹5,60,000. Find the variance in ₹ and %.

quiz.q: Spending more than the cost budget is…

lessons.title: Inflation and real returns
lessons.summary: Your true gain is what's left after inflation.

term.meaning: Return adjusted for inflation: (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1.

sections.b: Nominal return is the stated rate. Inflation reduces purchasing power. Real return ≈ nominal − inflation (approximation); exact formula uses division. Negative real returns mean you lose purchasing power.
Companies set prices, wages and investment hurdles with inflation in mind; investors judge returns in real terms.

lessons.example: An FD paying 6% when inflation is 6% gives roughly zero real return. Your money keeps pace, but doesn't grow.

calc.problem: Nominal return 8%; inflation 6%. Find the exact real return.

quiz.q: If inflation exceeds your return, your real return is…
The quick approximation for real return is…
Which body targets inflation in India?

lessons.title: Effective annual rate
lessons.summary: Compounding frequency changes the true cost of a loan.

term.meaning: The actual yearly rate after compounding: (1 + r/m)^m − 1.

sections.b: A loan quoted at 12% per year compounded monthly charges 1% a month, but compounding makes the true annual rate higher than 12%. More frequent compounding → higher EAR.
Comparing loans, credit cards and deposits fairly requires converting all rates to EAR.

lessons.example: Credit cards charging about 3.5% a month have an EAR above 50%, far higher than they look.

calc.problem: A loan charges 12% per year compounded monthly. What is the effective annual rate?

lessons.title: Annuities
lessons.summary: Value a stream of equal payments.

term.meaning: A series of equal payments at regular intervals for a fixed period.

sections.b: PV of an ordinary annuity = PMT × [1 − (1 + r)^−n] ÷ r. Examples: EMIs, lease payments, pension payouts, coupon payments.
Annuities are everywhere in finance: loan pricing, lease valuation and retirement planning.

lessons.example: A company comparing a ₹10,000 yearly lease for 5 years against buying the asset uses the annuity formula.

calc.problem: What is the present value of ₹10,000 received at the end of each year for 5 years at 8%?

options: At the end of each period
At the start of each period

quiz.q: A higher discount rate makes an annuity's PV…

lessons.title: The power of SIPs (future value of an annuity)
lessons.summary: Small regular investments grow into large sums.

term.meaning: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals, usually monthly, in a mutual fund.

sections.b: FV of an annuity = PMT × [(1 + r)^n − 1] ÷ r. Regular investing benefits from compounding and rupee-cost averaging (buying more units when prices are low).
Companies use the same maths for sinking funds (saving to repay debt). Individuals use it for long-term goals.

lessons.example: ₹5,000 a month invested from age 25 to 55 at 12% a year can grow to about ₹1.7 crore.

calc.problem: ₹5,000 invested at the end of every month for 10 years at 12% per year (1% per month). Find the future value.

options: Buying fewer units when prices fall
Buying more units when prices are low
quiz.why: Fixed amount buys more at lower prices.

quiz.q: The biggest driver of SIP growth over decades is…
A sinking fund is used by companies to…

lessons.title: Perpetuities
lessons.summary: Valuing cash flows that last forever.

term.meaning: A constant cash flow that continues indefinitely; PV = Cash flow ÷ r.

sections.b: A perpetuity's value is simply CF ÷ r. A growing perpetuity is CF₁ ÷ (r − g). This is the maths behind terminal values and the dividend discount model.
Perpetuities help value stable businesses, preference shares and endowments.

lessons.example: A preference share paying ₹9 a year forever, with a required return of 9%, is worth ₹100.

calc.problem: An investment pays ₹5,000 every year forever. The required return is 10%. What is it worth today?

quiz.q: If required return rises, perpetuity value…

lessons.title: Shares and market capitalisation
lessons.summary: What a company is worth on the stock market.

term.meaning: Share price × number of shares outstanding.

sections.b: Face value is the nominal value printed on a share (e.g. ₹10). Market price is what investors pay. Market cap = price × shares. SEBI classifies large caps as the top 100 companies by market cap, mid caps as 101-250 and small caps as 251 onwards.
Market cap shows investor expectations of future earnings, not just current profits.

lessons.example: Two companies with the same profit can have very different market caps if investors expect one to grow faster.

calc.problem: A company has 10 crore shares trading at ₹250 each. What is its market capitalisation?

quiz.q: In SEBI's classification, large caps are…
Face value of a share is…
options: The nominal value printed on it

lessons.title: Dividends, yield and payout
lessons.summary: How much profit is returned to shareholders?

term.meaning: Annual dividend per share ÷ share price.

sections.b: Dividend per share (DPS) is the cash paid per share. Dividend yield = DPS ÷ price. Payout ratio = DPS ÷ EPS (or dividends ÷ net income). Mature firms pay more; growth firms reinvest.
Investors seeking income look at yield; payout ratio shows sustainability and reinvestment.

lessons.example: Large Indian IT services companies have often paid out most of their profits through dividends and buybacks.

calc.problem: DPS ₹12; share price ₹300; EPS ₹30. Find dividend yield and payout ratio.

options: All profit is paid as dividends

lessons.title: Bonds: coupons and current yield
lessons.summary: How fixed-income securities pay investors.

term.meaning: Annual interest paid by a bond as a percentage of its face value.

sections.b: A bond has a face value (e.g. ₹1,000), a coupon rate and a maturity date. Current yield = annual coupon ÷ market price. If a bond trades below face value (discount), its yield is higher than the coupon.
Companies raise debt by issuing bonds/debentures; treasurers and investors must understand pricing and yields.

lessons.example: Government securities (G-secs) are considered risk-free in rupee terms and serve as the benchmark for corporate bond yields.

calc.problem: A bond with face value ₹1,000 pays an 8% coupon and trades at ₹950. Find the current yield.

quiz.q: If a bond trades below face value, its yield is…
In India, the benchmark risk-free bonds are…

lessons.title: Bond prices and interest rates
lessons.summary: When rates rise, bond prices fall.

term.meaning: The total annual return if a bond is held to maturity; the discount rate that equates price with future cash flows.

sections.b: Bond price = PV of coupons + PV of face value, discounted at the market yield. If market yields rise above the coupon, the bond's price falls below face value, and vice versa.
Banks and treasuries holding bonds face mark-to-market losses when RBI raises rates.

lessons.example: When yields rose sharply in 2022, many banks globally reported losses on their bond portfolios.

calc.problem: A 3-year bond, face value ₹1,000, 8% annual coupon. The market yield is 10%. What is its price?

quiz.q: When market interest rates rise, bond prices…
If YTM equals the coupon rate, the bond trades at…
A bond's price is the PV of…

lessons.title: GST basics for businesses
lessons.summary: How input tax credit makes GST a tax on value added.

term.meaning: GST paid on purchases that can be set off against GST collected on sales.

sections.b: GST is charged at each stage of supply. Businesses collect output GST on sales and claim credit for GST paid on inputs. Net GST payable = Output GST − ITC. Common rates: 5%, 12%, 18% and 28% (rates are revised periodically by the GST Council).
GST affects pricing, cash flow and compliance. Missed ITC is a direct cost; delays in claiming tie up working capital.

lessons.example: A consultancy billing ₹1 lakh + 18% GST collects ₹18,000 but can deduct GST it paid on software subscriptions.

calc.problem: A firm sells services worth ₹1,00,000 + 18% GST. It paid ₹9,000 GST on its inputs. Find invoice value and net GST payable.

options: GST paid on purchases set off against output GST

quiz.q: Who decides GST rate changes in India?

lessons.title: Inventory valuation: FIFO vs weighted average
lessons.summary: The method you choose changes reported profit.

term.meaning: First In, First Out: oldest inventory costs are expensed first.

sections.b: FIFO assumes the earliest purchases are sold first. Weighted average uses the average cost of all units available. Ind AS 2 allows FIFO or weighted average (not LIFO). In rising prices, FIFO gives lower COGS and higher profit.
Inventory method affects margins, taxes and comparisons between companies.

lessons.example: A retailer buying at rising prices reports higher gross profit under FIFO than under weighted average.

calc.problem: Bought 100 units at ₹10, then 100 units at ₹12. Sold 150 units. Find COGS under FIFO and weighted average.

quiz.q: Under FIFO, which costs are expensed first?
When prices rise, FIFO profit is usually…
Which method is NOT allowed under Ind AS 2?

lessons.title: Receivables and DSO
lessons.summary: How long customers take to pay you.

term.meaning: (Receivables ÷ Revenue) × 365; average days to collect cash from customers.

sections.b: High DSO means cash is stuck with customers. Businesses manage DSO through credit terms, reminders, early-payment discounts and credit checks.
Lower DSO improves cash flow and reduces bad-debt risk. MSMEs in India often struggle with delayed payments from large buyers.

lessons.example: The MSME Samadhaan portal and TReDS platforms help small businesses address delayed payments and finance receivables.

calc.problem: Receivables ₹15 lakh; annual revenue ₹1.2 crore. Find DSO.

quiz.q: A way to reduce DSO is…

lessons.title: Inventory turnover and DIO
lessons.summary: How fast stock is sold.

term.meaning: COGS ÷ Average inventory; times inventory is sold and replaced in a year.

sections.b: Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO) = 365 ÷ Inventory turnover. Higher turnover means leaner operations; too high can risk stock-outs.
Inventory ties up cash and can become obsolete. Retail and FMCG businesses obsess over turnover.

lessons.example: Fast-fashion retailers turn inventory many times a year; a jewellery store turns it slowly.

calc.problem: COGS ₹90 lakh; average inventory ₹15 lakh. Find inventory turnover and DIO.

quiz.q: A risk of very low inventory is…

lessons.title: Asset turnover and ROA
lessons.summary: How efficiently assets generate sales and profit.

term.meaning: Net income ÷ Total assets.

sections.b: Asset turnover = Sales ÷ Total assets. ROA = Net margin × Asset turnover. Asset-light businesses (software, platforms) typically have high turnover.
ROA shows how well management uses all resources, regardless of financing.

lessons.example: A supermarket earns thin margins but high asset turnover; a power utility has low turnover but steady margins.

calc.problem: Sales ₹50 crore; total assets ₹25 crore; net income ₹4 crore. Find asset turnover and ROA.

lessons.title: How the three statements connect
lessons.summary: Profit, balance sheet and cash flow are one linked system.

term.meaning: Cumulative profits kept in the business after dividends.

sections.b: Net income from the P&L flows into retained earnings on the balance sheet (minus dividends) and is the starting point of the cash flow statement. Ending cash on the cash flow statement equals cash on the balance sheet.
Understanding linkages helps you build financial models and spot accounting errors.

lessons.example: If a model's balance sheet doesn't balance, the error usually lies in a broken link between statements.

calc.problem: Opening retained earnings ₹200 crore; net income ₹50 crore; dividends ₹20 crore. Find closing retained earnings.
steps: Closing RE = Opening + Net income − Dividends

quiz.q: Net income flows to which balance sheet item?
The cash flow statement usually starts with…
Ending cash on the cash flow statement should equal…

lessons.title: Net Present Value (NPV)
lessons.summary: The gold standard for evaluating investments.

term.meaning: Sum of discounted future cash flows minus the initial investment.

sections.b: NPV = Σ CFt / (1 + r)^t − Initial investment. If NPV > 0, the project earns more than the required return and creates value.
Capital budgeting decisions (new plants, products, acquisitions) rely on NPV because it accounts for the time value of money and risk.

lessons.example: A ₹1 crore solar project with a positive NPV at a 10% cost of capital adds value to the firm.

calc.problem: Initial investment ₹1,000; cash flows ₹400, ₹500, ₹600 in years 1-3; discount rate 10%. Find NPV.

quiz.q: A project with negative NPV should generally be…
quiz.why: It destroys value at the required return.

quiz.q: Which discount rate is typically used for NPV of an average project?

options: Time value of money and risk

lessons.title: Internal Rate of Return (IRR)
lessons.summary: The project's own rate of return.

term.meaning: The discount rate that makes NPV equal zero.

sections.b: Find the rate where NPV = 0 (trial and error or a calculator). Accept if IRR > cost of capital (hurdle rate).
IRR is intuitive (a percentage) and widely used in private equity and corporate finance, but can mislead with unusual cash flows or when comparing projects of different sizes.

lessons.example: If a project's IRR is 18% and the company's WACC is 11%, it clears the hurdle.

calc.problem: Initial investment ₹1,000; cash flows ₹400, ₹500, ₹600. Estimate IRR.

quiz.q: Accept a project when IRR is…
quiz.why: It must beat the hurdle rate.

options: Cash flows change sign multiple times

lessons.title: Payback period
lessons.summary: How quickly do you get your money back?

term.meaning: Time required for cumulative cash inflows to recover the initial investment.

sections.b: Add cash flows year by year until the investment is recovered. Payback = years before full recovery + unrecovered amount / cash flow in recovery year.
Simple measure of liquidity and risk. Popular with small businesses. Weakness: ignores time value and cash flows after payback.

lessons.example: A ₹6 lakh machine saving ₹2 lakh a year pays back in 3 years.

calc.problem: Initial investment ₹1,000; cash flows ₹300, ₹400, ₹500. Find the payback period.

quiz.q: A key weakness of the payback method is that it…
options: Ignores cash flows after the payback point
quiz.why: It also ignores the time value of money (in its simple form).
And time value in simple form.

quiz.q: Payback is popular because it is…

lessons.title: Cost of equity (CAPM)
lessons.summary: What return do shareholders expect?

term.meaning: Measure of a stock's sensitivity to market movements; β = 1 moves with the market.

sections.b: CAPM: Re = Rf + β × (Rm − Rf). Rf = risk-free rate (e.g. 10-year G-sec), (Rm − Rf) = market risk premium. Higher beta → higher required return.
Cost of equity feeds into WACC and valuation. Equity is usually more expensive than debt because shareholders bear more risk.

lessons.example: A high-beta tech stock (β = 1.5) needs a higher expected return than a utility stock (β = 0.6).

calc.problem: Risk-free rate 7%, beta 1.2, expected market return 12%. Find the cost of equity.

options: Twice as volatile as the market
quiz.why: Beta < 1 means smaller moves than the market.

quiz.q: A typical Indian proxy for the risk-free rate is…

lessons.title: After-tax cost of debt
lessons.summary: Interest is tax-deductible, so debt is cheaper than it looks.

term.meaning: Tax saved because interest expense reduces taxable income.

sections.b: After-tax cost of debt = Rd × (1 − Tax rate). Rd is usually the yield on the company's debt or its borrowing rate.
This tax advantage is why companies use some debt. It reduces WACC up to the point where financial risk rises.

lessons.example: A company paying ₹10 crore interest at a 25% tax rate saves ₹2.5 crore in tax.

calc.problem: A company borrows at 9% and pays tax at 25%. What is the after-tax cost of debt?

quiz.q: Why is the after-tax cost of debt lower than the interest rate?
quiz.why: The tax shield reduces the effective cost.

quiz.q: At a 30% tax rate, 10% debt costs after tax…
The tax shield on ₹100 interest at 25% tax is…

lessons.title: WACC
lessons.summary: The minimum return a company must earn on its investments.

term.meaning: Weighted Average Cost of Capital: cost of each funding source weighted by its share.

sections.b: WACC = E/V × Re + D/V × Rd × (1 − T), where V = E + D (market values). It is used as the discount rate for the firm's average-risk projects.
If a project returns less than WACC, it destroys value. Lower WACC → higher valuations.

lessons.example: A company funded 60% by equity at 13% and 40% by debt at 6.75% after tax has a WACC of 10.5%.

calc.problem: Equity ₹600 cr at 13%; Debt ₹400 cr at 9% pre-tax; Tax 25%. Find WACC.

options: The discount rate for average-risk projects
quiz.why: It reflects the blended cost of capital.

quiz.q: If a company adds cheaper debt (within limits), WACC usually…

lessons.title: Liquidity ratios
lessons.summary: Can the company pay its short-term bills?

term.meaning: (Current assets − Inventory) / Current liabilities; a stricter liquidity test.

sections.b: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities. Quick (acid-test) ratio excludes inventory because it may be hard to sell quickly. Cash ratio uses only cash and equivalents.
Suppliers and lenders check liquidity before giving credit. Too low = risk; too high = idle resources.

lessons.example: A manufacturer with lots of slow-moving inventory may have a fine current ratio but a weak quick ratio.

calc.problem: Current assets ₹500 lakh (incl. inventory ₹150 lakh); Current liabilities ₹250 lakh. Find current and quick ratios.

quiz.why: Inventory is the least liquid current asset.

options: Liquid assets cover current liabilities 1.4 times

lessons.title: Leverage and coverage
lessons.summary: How much debt, and can the company service it?

term.meaning: EBIT / Interest expense: times interest is covered by operating profit.

sections.b: Debt-to-equity (D/E) = Total debt / Equity. Interest coverage = EBIT / Interest. Net debt = Debt − Cash. Net debt/EBITDA is a common lender metric.
Leverage magnifies returns in good times and losses in bad times. Rating agencies and banks set limits on these ratios.

lessons.example: Lenders may require interest coverage above 3x and net debt/EBITDA below 3x as loan covenants.

calc.problem: Debt ₹400 cr; Equity ₹800 cr; EBIT ₹300 cr; Interest ₹60 cr. Find D/E and interest coverage.

options: Little room to service debt if profits fall

quiz.q: A common lender covenant limit is net debt/EBITDA below about…

lessons.title: ROE and DuPont analysis
lessons.summary: Break return on equity into its drivers.

term.meaning: Net income / Shareholders' equity.

sections.b: DuPont: ROE = Net margin × Asset turnover × Equity multiplier = (NI/Sales) × (Sales/Assets) × (Assets/Equity). It shows whether ROE comes from profitability, efficiency or leverage.
Two companies with 15% ROE can be very different: one highly profitable, another heavily leveraged.

lessons.example: Asian Paints' high ROE is driven by strong margins, while a retailer might rely on high asset turnover.

calc.problem: Net income ₹120 cr; Sales ₹1,500 cr; Assets ₹2,000 cr; Equity ₹800 cr. Compute ROE using DuPont.

quiz.q: DuPont helps identify whether ROE comes from…

lessons.title: Cash conversion cycle
lessons.summary: Days between paying suppliers and collecting from customers.

term.meaning: Days Sales Outstanding: average days to collect receivables.

sections.b: CCC = DIO (days inventory outstanding) + DSO (days sales outstanding) − DPO (days payables outstanding). Shorter cycle = less cash tied up.
Improving CCC frees cash without new financing. Companies like Amazon even run negative cycles.

lessons.example: D-Mart's fast inventory turnover and quick supplier payments are part of its strategic model.

calc.problem: DIO 45 days; DSO 30 days; DPO 40 days. Find the cash conversion cycle.

quiz.q: Which change shortens the cash conversion cycle?
A negative cash conversion cycle means…
options: Customers pay before suppliers are paid

lessons.title: Operating leverage
lessons.summary: How fixed costs magnify profit changes.

term.meaning: % change in EBIT / % change in sales = Contribution / EBIT.

sections.b: High fixed costs mean small changes in sales cause big changes in operating profit. DOL = Contribution margin / EBIT.
Airlines and software firms have high operating leverage: great in booms, painful in downturns.

lessons.example: An airline with mostly fixed costs sees profits soar when planes fill up and collapse when demand drops.

calc.problem: Sales ₹1,000; Variable costs ₹600; Fixed costs ₹250. Find DOL and the EBIT change if sales rise 10%.

quiz.q: A company with high fixed costs has…
High operating leverage is risky in…

lessons.title: Loan amortisation and EMI
lessons.summary: How loan repayments split between interest and principal.

term.meaning: Paying off a loan through regular instalments covering interest and principal.

sections.b: EMI = P × r × (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n − 1), with r = monthly rate. Early EMIs are mostly interest; later EMIs are mostly principal.
Companies and individuals use amortisation schedules to plan cash flows and compare loan offers.

lessons.example: Prepaying a home loan early saves far more interest than prepaying late, because interest is front-loaded.

calc.problem: Loan ₹10,00,000 at 9% annual interest for 10 years (120 months). Find the EMI and total interest.

quiz.q: In early EMIs, most of the payment goes to…
quiz.why: Interest is charged on a large outstanding balance.

quiz.q: Prepaying a loan early saves the most interest because…

lessons.title: Relevant cash flows and sunk costs
lessons.summary: Only future, incremental cash flows matter for decisions.

term.meaning: Money already spent that cannot be recovered; irrelevant to future decisions.

sections.b: Relevant cash flows are incremental: they change because of the decision. Ignore sunk costs, include opportunity costs, side effects (cannibalisation) and working capital needs. Operating cash flow = (Revenue − Costs − Depreciation) × (1 − T) + Depreciation.
Including sunk costs (or ignoring opportunity costs) leads to wrong investment decisions. This is the 'sunk cost fallacy'.

lessons.example: A company spent ₹5 lakh on a market study. Whether to launch the product should ignore that ₹5 lakh; it's spent either way.

calc.problem: A new project adds revenue of ₹30 lakh and cash costs of ₹18 lakh a year. Depreciation is ₹4 lakh; tax 25%. A feasibility study already cost ₹5 lakh. Find annual operating cash flow.

quiz.why: It doesn't change with the decision.

options: Opportunity cost of using an owned building

quiz.q: Why add back depreciation in OCF?
options: It's a non-cash expense that reduced taxable profit

lessons.title: Profitability index
lessons.summary: Value created per rupee invested, which is useful under capital rationing.

term.meaning: PV of future cash flows ÷ Initial investment.

sections.b: PI > 1 means positive NPV. When capital is limited, rank projects by PI to maximise total NPV per rupee of budget.
Companies often have more good ideas than capital. PI helps allocate a fixed budget.

lessons.example: With a ₹10 crore budget, choosing three projects with PI 1.4, 1.3 and 1.25 may beat one big project with PI 1.1.

calc.problem: PV of future cash flows ₹1,227.65; initial investment ₹1,000. Find the profitability index.

lessons.title: Discounted payback period
lessons.summary: Payback that respects the time value of money.

term.meaning: Time until cumulative discounted cash flows recover the initial investment.

sections.b: Discount each year's cash flow, accumulate them, and find when the total reaches the investment. It is always longer than simple payback.
It adds time value to a quick liquidity measure, which is useful for risky or fast-changing industries.

lessons.example: A tech project with fast obsolescence might require discounted payback under 3 years.

calc.problem: Investment ₹1,000; cash flows ₹400, ₹500, ₹600; discount rate 10%. Find the discounted payback.

quiz.q: A remaining weakness of discounted payback is…
options: It ignores cash flows after payback

lessons.title: When NPV and IRR disagree
lessons.summary: For mutually exclusive projects, trust NPV.

term.meaning: Choosing one project rules out the other.

sections.b: IRR measures percentage return; NPV measures value in rupees. A small project can have a higher IRR but create less value. Conflicts arise from scale and timing differences. NPV maximises shareholder wealth.
Choosing by IRR alone can leave money on the table.

lessons.example: Would you prefer a 50% return on ₹100 or a 20% return on ₹1 crore? The second creates far more value.

calc.problem: Project A: invest ₹100, receive ₹130 in a year (IRR 30%). Project B: invest ₹500, receive ₹600 in a year (IRR 20%). Discount rate 10%. Which creates more value?
steps: B has lower IRR but higher NPV

quiz.q: For mutually exclusive projects, prefer the one with higher…

lessons.title: Sensitivity analysis
lessons.summary: Which assumptions could break your project?

term.meaning: Changing one input at a time to see its effect on NPV or profit.

sections.b: Vary key inputs (volume, price, costs, discount rate) by ±10-20% and observe NPV. Inputs with the biggest impact deserve the most research and risk management. Tornado charts visualise this.
It shows decision-makers where the risks are concentrated before committing capital.

lessons.example: If a 10% price drop makes NPV negative, pricing power becomes the critical question.

calc.problem: Base case: PV of inflows ₹1,227.65, investment ₹1,000, NPV ₹227.65. What is NPV if all cash inflows are 10% lower?

options: Which inputs most affect the result

quiz.q: If a small change flips NPV negative, the project is…

lessons.title: Cost of preference shares
lessons.summary: The cost of a hybrid between debt and equity.

term.meaning: Shares with a fixed dividend paid before ordinary shareholders, usually without voting rights.

sections.b: Cost of preference capital Rp = Preference dividend ÷ Net issue price. Unlike interest, preference dividends are not tax-deductible.
Preference capital is part of the capital structure and enters WACC with its own weight and cost.

lessons.example: Banks and NBFCs sometimes issue preference shares to raise capital without diluting voting control.

calc.problem: Preference shares with face value ₹100 pay a 9% dividend and are issued at ₹100 (no costs). What is the cost of preference capital?

quiz.q: Are preference dividends tax-deductible for the company?

lessons.title: Estimating beta
lessons.summary: Measuring how a stock moves with the market.

term.meaning: A measure of how two variables move together.

sections.b: Beta = Covariance(stock, market) ÷ Variance(market). It is usually estimated by regressing stock returns on index returns (e.g. Nifty 50) over 2-5 years of weekly or monthly data.
Beta drives cost of equity via CAPM. Analysts often adjust or use industry betas for stability.

lessons.example: Defensive sectors like FMCG tend to have betas below 1; cyclical sectors like metals often exceed 1.

calc.problem: Covariance of a stock's returns with the market = 0.012; variance of market returns = 0.010. Find beta.

quiz.q: A cyclical metals company likely has beta…
Indian betas are commonly measured against…

lessons.title: Cost of equity from the dividend growth model
lessons.summary: An alternative to CAPM for dividend payers.

term.meaning: Re = D₁ ÷ P₀ + g; required return implied by price, next dividend and growth.

sections.b: Rearranging the Gordon model gives the market's implied cost of equity: dividend yield plus expected growth.
Comparing CAPM and DGM estimates gives a sanity check on cost of equity.

lessons.example: A utility with a 5% dividend yield and 6% expected growth implies about an 11% cost of equity.

calc.problem: Next year's dividend ₹6; current price ₹120; expected growth 7%. Find the cost of equity.

options: As a sanity check on estimates

lessons.title: Financial leverage and EPS
lessons.summary: Debt magnifies shareholder returns, both ways.

term.meaning: EBIT ÷ (EBIT − Interest); % change in EPS for 1% change in EBIT.

sections.b: EPS = (EBIT − Interest) × (1 − T) ÷ Shares. With fixed interest, a rise in EBIT boosts EPS disproportionately, but a fall hurts more.
Financial leverage decisions trade higher expected EPS for higher risk.

lessons.example: A highly leveraged real-estate developer sees profits swing wildly as sales cycle up and down.

calc.problem: EBIT ₹200 crore; interest ₹50 crore; tax 25%; 10 crore shares. Find EPS and DFL.

quiz.q: DFL of 1.33 means a 10% rise in EBIT raises EPS by about…

lessons.title: Combined leverage
lessons.summary: Operating plus financial leverage: total risk magnification.

term.meaning: DOL × DFL; % change in EPS for 1% change in sales.

sections.b: DCL links sales changes directly to EPS changes. High fixed costs (operating leverage) plus high debt (financial leverage) make earnings very sensitive.
Companies with high operating leverage often choose lower debt to keep total risk manageable.

lessons.example: Airlines combine high fixed costs and heavy debt, so a small demand drop can wipe out profits.

calc.problem: DOL = 2.0 and DFL = 1.5. If sales rise 10%, by how much does EPS change?

quiz.q: A firm with high operating leverage should usually prefer…
DCL of 3 and a 10% sales fall means EPS falls by about…

lessons.title: Cost of skipping a cash discount
lessons.summary: Trade credit can be surprisingly expensive.

term.meaning: A reduction offered for paying early, e.g. '2/10 net 30'.

sections.b: '2/10 net 30' means 2% discount if paid within 10 days; otherwise full amount in 30 days. Annualised cost of skipping = (Discount ÷ (100 − Discount)) × (365 ÷ (Credit days − Discount days)).
If borrowing is cheaper than the implied cost, take the discount, which often boosts profit.

lessons.example: Paying suppliers early using a 10% working capital loan to capture a 37% implied return is a smart move.

calc.problem: Terms: 2/10 net 30. What is the annualised cost of not taking the discount?

options: 2% discount if paid in 10 days, else full by day 30

quiz.q: If your bank loan costs 11%, should you take a discount costing 37% to skip?
The annualised cost of skipping a 2/10 net 30 discount is roughly…

lessons.title: Economic order quantity (EOQ)
lessons.summary: How much to order to minimise inventory costs.

term.meaning: √(2DS ÷ H): the order size that minimises total ordering plus holding cost.

sections.b: D = annual demand, S = cost per order, H = holding cost per unit per year. Ordering too often raises ordering costs; ordering too much raises holding costs. EOQ balances them.
Inventory decisions affect working capital, storage costs and service levels.

lessons.example: A pharma distributor uses EOQ (adjusted for safety stock) to plan reorders of fast-moving medicines.

calc.problem: Annual demand 12,000 units; ordering cost ₹500 per order; holding cost ₹20 per unit per year. Find EOQ.
calc.answer: ≈ 775 units per order (≈ 15.5 orders a year)

options: Protect against demand or supply uncertainty

lessons.title: Cash budgeting
lessons.summary: Forecast cash month by month to avoid surprises.

term.meaning: A forecast of cash receipts and payments to project cash balances and financing needs.

sections.b: Closing cash = Opening cash + Receipts − Payments. Compare with a minimum cash balance to see when you need to borrow or can invest surplus.
Many profitable businesses fail from cash shortages. Cash budgets give early warning.

lessons.example: Retailers build cash budgets to fund inventory before Diwali and repay loans after the festive season.

calc.problem: Opening cash ₹5 lakh; expected receipts ₹20 lakh; payments ₹23 lakh. Minimum cash balance required ₹3 lakh. How much must the firm borrow?

quiz.q: Why keep a minimum cash balance?
options: As a buffer against unexpected needs

lessons.title: Factoring and invoice discounting
lessons.summary: Turn receivables into cash today.

term.meaning: Selling receivables to a financier (factor) for immediate cash, minus fees.

sections.b: A factor advances a percentage (e.g. 80-90%) of invoice value, charges a fee/discount, and may collect from customers. Invoice discounting is similar but the business keeps collection. TReDS enables this for MSMEs in India.
Factoring improves liquidity without traditional loans, but has a cost.

lessons.example: An MSME supplying a large automaker uses TReDS to get paid in days instead of waiting 90 days.

calc.problem: Receivables of ₹10 lakh are factored at an 85% advance with a 2% fee on invoice value. How much cash is received now, and what is the fee?
steps: Balance (minus fee) is paid when the customer pays

quiz.q: A key benefit of factoring is…

lessons.title: Lease or buy?
lessons.summary: Compare the present value cost of each option.

term.meaning: A contract to use an asset in exchange for periodic payments.

sections.b: Compare PV of lease payments with the purchase price (adjusted for tax effects and residual value in a full analysis). Under Ind AS 116, most leases appear on the balance sheet as right-of-use assets and lease liabilities.
Lease vs buy decisions affect cash, flexibility and reported debt.

lessons.example: Many retail chains lease stores to keep flexibility and conserve capital for expansion.

calc.problem: An asset costs ₹5,20,000 to buy, or ₹2,00,000 a year (end of year) to lease for 3 years. Discount rate 10%. Ignoring taxes and residual value, which is cheaper?

quiz.q: Under Ind AS 116, most leases are…
options: Recognised as right-of-use assets and lease liabilities

quiz.q: To compare lease vs buy, compare…
options: PV of lease payments with purchase cost

lessons.title: Target profit analysis
lessons.summary: How many units to hit a profit goal?

term.meaning: The desired profit level used to calculate required sales volume.

sections.b: Required units = (Fixed costs + Target profit) ÷ Contribution margin per unit. Required revenue = (Fixed costs + Target profit) ÷ CM ratio.
Sales targets, pricing and incentive plans are built from this calculation.

lessons.example: A startup aiming for ₹10 lakh monthly profit can tell its sales team exactly how many subscriptions to sell.

calc.problem: Fixed costs ₹2,00,000; contribution margin ₹200 per unit; target profit ₹1,00,000. How many units must be sold?

options: (Fixed costs + Target profit) ÷ CM per unit

quiz.q: If CM per unit rises, required units…

lessons.title: Margin of safety
lessons.summary: How far sales can fall before losses begin.

term.meaning: (Actual sales − Break-even sales) ÷ Actual sales.

sections.b: A higher margin of safety means a business can absorb more sales decline before losing money. It can be expressed in units, revenue or percentage.
Lenders and managers use it as a quick risk indicator.

lessons.example: A restaurant with a 10% margin of safety is fragile; one with 40% can survive a slow season.

calc.problem: Actual sales 1,500 units; break-even 1,000 units. Find the margin of safety.

quiz.q: A higher margin of safety means…
Raising fixed costs usually makes MOS…

lessons.title: Price and volume variance
lessons.summary: Explain why revenue differed from budget.

term.meaning: Revenue impact of selling more or fewer units than budgeted, at budget price.

sections.b: Volume variance = (Actual units − Budget units) × Budget price. Price variance = (Actual price − Budget price) × Actual units. Together they explain total revenue variance.
Separating price from volume tells management whether to fix pricing or sales effort.

lessons.example: A company may hit revenue targets only by discounting heavily: a favourable volume variance hiding an unfavourable price variance.

calc.problem: Budget: 1,000 units at ₹50 (₹50,000). Actual: 1,100 units at ₹48 (₹52,800). Find volume and price variances.
calc.answer: Volume +₹5,000 F; price −₹2,200 U; total +₹2,800 F

quiz.q: Selling at a lower price than budget creates…

options: To identify the real driver of performance

lessons.title: Return on capital employed (ROCE)
lessons.summary: How efficiently a business uses its long-term capital.

term.meaning: Total assets − Current liabilities (or Equity + Non-current debt).

sections.b: ROCE = EBIT ÷ Capital employed. Because it uses EBIT (pre-interest), it compares companies with different financing. Compare ROCE with the cost of capital.
Investors like businesses with high, stable ROCE. It signals a competitive advantage.

lessons.example: Companies with strong brands or network effects often sustain ROCE well above 20%.

calc.problem: EBIT ₹300 crore; total assets ₹2,000 crore; current liabilities ₹500 crore. Find ROCE.

lessons.title: ROIC vs WACC: the value spread
lessons.summary: Growth only creates value when returns beat the cost of capital.

term.meaning: Return on Invested Capital = NOPAT ÷ Invested capital.

sections.b: Value spread = ROIC − WACC. Economic profit = Spread × Invested capital. Growth with ROIC below WACC destroys value, however impressive revenue looks.
This is the single most important idea in corporate valuation and capital allocation.

lessons.example: A company growing 30% a year with ROIC of 6% and WACC of 11% is shrinking shareholder value.

calc.problem: NOPAT ₹150 crore; invested capital ₹1,000 crore; WACC 11%. Find ROIC, spread and economic profit.

lessons.title: Credit ratings and spreads
lessons.summary: How lenders price default risk.

term.meaning: Extra yield over a risk-free government bond to compensate for default risk.

sections.b: Rating agencies (CRISIL, ICRA, CARE, India Ratings) grade issuers from AAA (highest safety) downwards; BBB- and above is investment grade. Lower ratings mean higher spreads and borrowing costs. Spreads are measured in basis points (1 bp = 0.01%).
A rating upgrade can cut interest costs significantly; a downgrade can trigger covenant breaches.

lessons.example: After the IL&FS default in 2018, spreads for many NBFCs widened sharply as investors repriced risk.

calc.problem: A corporate bond yields 9.2%; a G-sec of similar maturity yields 7.1%. Find the credit spread in basis points.

quiz.q: A lower credit rating usually means…
Which is an Indian rating agency?

lessons.title: Interest rate risk on loans
lessons.summary: How a change in rates hits your interest bill.

term.meaning: An interest rate that resets with a benchmark (e.g. repo-linked or MCLR).

sections.b: On floating-rate debt, a rise in the benchmark directly raises interest expense. Extra interest = Loan × Rate change. Companies manage this with fixed-rate debt or interest rate swaps.
Treasurers must model rate scenarios: a 1% rise on large borrowings can wipe out a big share of profit.

lessons.example: When RBI raised the repo rate by 250 bps in 2022-23, floating-rate borrowers saw EMIs and interest costs jump.

calc.problem: A company has a ₹100 crore floating-rate loan. Rates rise by 50 basis points. How much extra annual interest does it pay?

quiz.q: A tool to fix a floating rate is…
Floating-rate borrowers are hurt when rates…

lessons.title: Free cash flow to firm (FCFF)
lessons.summary: The cash available to all investors after reinvestment.

term.meaning: Net Operating Profit After Tax = EBIT × (1 − Tax rate).

sections.b: FCFF = EBIT × (1 − T) + D&A − Capex − Increase in net working capital. It is the cash available to both debt and equity holders.
FCFF is the foundation of DCF valuation. Growing companies may show profit but negative FCF due to heavy investment.

lessons.example: A fast-growing EV maker can have rising EBIT but negative FCFF because it is building factories.

calc.problem: EBIT ₹500 cr; Tax 25%; D&A ₹80 cr; Capex ₹150 cr; Increase in NWC ₹30 cr. Find FCFF.

quiz.q: Which item reduces free cash flow?
quiz.why: Capex is cash spent on long-term assets.

quiz.q: FCFF is the cash available to…
An increase in net working capital ___ FCFF.

lessons.title: Terminal value (Gordon growth)
lessons.summary: Valuing all cash flows beyond the forecast period.

term.meaning: Value of a business beyond the explicit forecast, assuming stable growth forever.

sections.b: Gordon growth: TV = FCF(next year) / (WACC − g). g must be below WACC and sustainable (often ≈ long-term GDP/inflation growth). TV often makes up 60-80% of a DCF value.
Small changes in g or WACC can swing valuations enormously, so always run sensitivity tables.

lessons.example: Changing g from 4% to 5% with WACC 10% raises TV by 20% (1/0.06 → 1/0.05).

calc.problem: Next year's FCF ₹110 cr, WACC 10%, perpetual growth 4%. Find the terminal value.

quiz.q: In the Gordon growth model, g must be…
A reasonable perpetual growth rate is close to…
options: Long-term nominal GDP growth or lower

lessons.title: DCF valuation
lessons.summary: Value = present value of all future free cash flows.

term.meaning: Valuation method that discounts projected free cash flows and a terminal value at WACC.

sections.b: Steps: 1) forecast FCFF for 3-10 years, 2) compute terminal value, 3) discount everything at WACC, 4) sum to get enterprise value.
DCF estimates intrinsic value based on fundamentals, used in M&A, equity research and investment decisions.

lessons.example: Analysts value companies like TCS by forecasting cash flows and discounting them, then comparing with the market price.

calc.problem: FCFF: Y1 ₹100, Y2 ₹110, Y3 ₹121 cr; WACC 10%; growth after Y3 = 3%. Find enterprise value.

quiz.q: In a typical DCF, which part often contributes the most value?
quiz.why: TV often accounts for most of the value.

quiz.q: DCF value is highly sensitive to…

lessons.title: Enterprise value vs equity value
lessons.summary: From the value of the business to the value per share.

term.meaning: Value of the whole business to all capital providers = Equity value + Net debt.

sections.b: Equity value = EV − Debt + Cash (i.e. EV − Net debt). Per-share value = Equity value / Shares outstanding.
DCF gives EV; investors care about share price. M&A buyers pay for equity but also take on debt.

lessons.example: Buying a house worth ₹1 crore with a ₹60 lakh mortgage: the 'equity' you pay the seller is ₹40 lakh, but the 'EV' is ₹1 crore.

calc.problem: EV ₹5,000 cr; Debt ₹1,500 cr; Cash ₹300 cr; 100 crore shares. Find equity value per share.

quiz.why: Subtract what's owed to lenders, add back cash.

lessons.title: Valuation multiples (EV/EBITDA, P/E)
lessons.summary: Value a company by comparing it with peers.

term.meaning: Enterprise value divided by EBITDA; a capital-structure-neutral multiple.

sections.b: Relative valuation: find comparable companies, compute their multiples, apply the median to your company's metric. Common: EV/EBITDA, P/E, EV/Sales.
Quick, market-based and widely used in investment banking. But it assumes peers are fairly valued.

lessons.example: If listed peers trade at 8x EV/EBITDA, a similar private company with ₹250 cr EBITDA might be worth around ₹2,000 cr EV.

calc.problem: Peer median EV/EBITDA 8x; target EBITDA ₹250 cr; net debt ₹400 cr. Find EV and equity value.

quiz.q: Why is EV/EBITDA useful for comparing companies?
options: It is neutral to capital structure
quiz.why: Both EV and EBITDA are before financing effects.

lessons.title: Capital structure and the tax shield
lessons.summary: How debt can add value, up to a point.

term.meaning: Theory: without taxes, capital structure doesn't change firm value; with taxes, debt adds value via the tax shield.

sections.b: Value of levered firm = Value unlevered + PV of tax shield. For permanent debt, PV of tax shield = D × T. Beyond a point, bankruptcy and distress costs outweigh benefits (trade-off theory).
CFOs choose a target debt level balancing tax benefits, flexibility and risk of financial distress.

lessons.example: Infrastructure firms with stable cash flows carry more debt than volatile tech firms.

calc.problem: Permanent debt ₹1,000 cr at 8%; tax rate 25%. Find the annual tax shield and its present value.

quiz.why: Distress costs eventually exceed tax benefits.

lessons.title: Dividend discount model
lessons.summary: Value a share by its future dividends.

term.meaning: Share of net income paid out as dividends.

sections.b: Gordon growth DDM: Price = D1 / (Re − g), where D1 = next year's dividend. Sustainable growth g ≈ ROE × Retention ratio.
Useful for stable dividend payers like utilities and FMCG companies.

lessons.example: A company with ROE 20% retaining 40% of profits can grow at about 8%.

calc.problem: Next year's dividend ₹5; cost of equity 12%; growth 5%. Find the share value.

quiz.q: DDM requires the cost of equity to be…

lessons.title: EPS and P/E
lessons.summary: Earnings per share and what the market pays for them.

term.meaning: Price per share / Earnings per share: how many rupees investors pay per rupee of earnings.

sections.b: EPS = Net income / Shares outstanding. P/E = Price / EPS. High P/E often signals high growth expectations (or overvaluation). Diluted EPS includes options and convertibles.
P/E is the most quoted valuation metric in equity markets and investor communication.

lessons.example: FMCG stocks often trade at higher P/Es than PSU banks because of steadier growth and higher ROE.

calc.problem: Net income ₹200 cr; 50 crore shares; sector P/E 15x. Find EPS and implied share price.

quiz.q: Issuing new shares without increasing profit will…
quiz.why: Same earnings spread over more shares.

lessons.title: Economic Value Added (EVA)
lessons.summary: Profit after charging for all capital used.

term.meaning: NOPAT − (WACC × Invested capital).

sections.b: A company truly creates value only if its return on invested capital (ROIC) exceeds WACC. EVA measures this surplus in rupees.
Used for performance management and executive compensation to encourage efficient use of capital.

lessons.example: A division earning 9% ROIC with a 12% WACC is accounting-profitable but destroying economic value.

calc.problem: NOPAT ₹375 cr; invested capital ₹3,000 cr; WACC 10%. Find ROIC and EVA.

quiz.why: Returns exceed the cost of capital.

quiz.q: A division with ROIC 9% and WACC 12% is…

lessons.title: Portfolio return and beta
lessons.summary: Combining assets changes risk and return.

term.meaning: Spreading investments to reduce unsystematic (company-specific) risk.

sections.b: Portfolio expected return = Σ weight × return. Portfolio beta = Σ weight × beta. Diversification reduces company-specific risk but not market (systematic) risk.
Corporate treasuries, pension funds and individuals manage risk using these principles.

lessons.example: Holding both an IT exporter and an importer can partly offset currency risk.

calc.problem: 60% in Stock A (expected return 12%, β 1.2) and 40% in Stock B (8%, β 0.8). Find portfolio return and beta.

lessons.title: Hedging currency risk with forwards
lessons.summary: Lock in exchange rates to protect margins.

term.meaning: Agreement to buy/sell currency at a fixed rate on a future date.

sections.b: Importers fear the rupee weakening; exporters fear it strengthening. A forward locks the rate, removing uncertainty (and also any upside).
Treasury teams hedge to protect budgets and margins; unhedged exposure can wipe out profits.

lessons.example: An Indian IT exporter sells USD forwards to lock in rupee revenue.

calc.problem: An importer must pay $1,00,000 in 3 months. Forward rate ₹84.50/$. At maturity spot is ₹86.00/$. How much did the hedge save?

quiz.q: An Indian importer paying in USD is hurt when…
quiz.why: More rupees are needed per dollar.

quiz.q: An exporter receiving USD fears the rupee…

lessons.title: Scenario analysis and expected NPV
lessons.summary: Plan for multiple futures, not just one forecast.

term.meaning: Probability-weighted average of possible outcomes.

sections.b: Build scenarios (bear, base, bull), assign probabilities, compute NPV in each, then the expected NPV = Σ probability × NPV. Sensitivity analysis changes one input at a time.
Helps leaders understand risk, downside protection and what drives value. Investment committees expect it.

lessons.example: Before launching in a new market, a company models low, medium and high demand cases.

calc.problem: Scenarios: Bear 30% probability NPV −₹200 cr; Base 50% NPV ₹300 cr; Bull 20% NPV ₹800 cr. Find expected NPV.

quiz.why: Scenario analysis changes several inputs together.

lessons.title: M&A synergies and the acquisition premium
lessons.summary: An acquisition creates value only if synergies exceed the premium paid.

term.meaning: Extra value from combining two firms: cost savings, revenue gains or financial benefits.

sections.b: Synergy = Value(combined) − Value(A) − Value(B). Premium = Price paid − Target's standalone value. NPV to the acquirer = Synergy − Premium. Many deals overpay because synergies are overestimated.
M&A is one of the largest capital allocation decisions a CEO makes, and research shows many acquisitions destroy acquirer value.

lessons.example: Merging two cement companies can cut logistics and procurement costs, a classic cost synergy.

calc.problem: Acquirer worth ₹1,000 crore; target worth ₹400 crore; combined worth ₹1,550 crore. The acquirer pays ₹480 crore. Find synergy, premium and NPV to the acquirer.

quiz.q: A common reason acquisitions fail is…

lessons.title: Accretion and dilution
lessons.summary: Will the deal raise or lower EPS?

term.meaning: A deal that increases the acquirer's EPS.

sections.b: Pro-forma EPS = (Acquirer NI + Target NI + synergies − financing costs) ÷ (Acquirer shares + new shares issued). If pro-forma EPS > current EPS, the deal is accretive; otherwise dilutive. A stock deal is usually accretive when the target's P/E is lower than the acquirer's.
Boards and markets watch EPS impact, though accretion doesn't guarantee value creation.

lessons.example: Paying with highly valued stock can make a deal accretive even if the price is high.

calc.problem: Acquirer: NI ₹100 crore, 50 crore shares (EPS ₹2.00). Target NI ₹30 crore. The acquirer issues 20 crore new shares. Find pro-forma EPS (ignore synergies).

quiz.q: In a stock deal, buying a target with a lower P/E is usually…

lessons.title: Leveraged buyouts (LBO)
lessons.summary: How private equity uses debt to amplify returns.

term.meaning: Multiple on Invested Capital = Exit equity value ÷ Equity invested.

sections.b: In an LBO, a PE fund buys a company using a large share of debt, improves operations, repays debt from cash flows and exits after 3-7 years. Returns come from EBITDA growth, multiple expansion and debt paydown.
LBO maths shows how leverage and cash generation drive equity returns, plus the risks if cash flows disappoint.

lessons.example: PE funds in India have bought controlling stakes in companies across healthcare, IT services and consumer brands.

calc.problem: A PE fund buys a company for ₹1,000 crore with ₹600 crore debt and ₹400 crore equity. After 5 years it sells for ₹1,400 crore, with debt reduced to ₹300 crore. Find MOIC and IRR.

options: EBITDA growth, multiple expansion and debt paydown
Cash flows too weak to service debt

lessons.title: Levered and unlevered beta
lessons.summary: Adjust beta for different capital structures.

term.meaning: Beta of the business without debt; reflects pure business risk.

sections.b: Hamada equation: βL = βU × [1 + (1 − T) × D/E]. Analysts unlever peer betas to remove their financing effects, average them, then relever at the target's capital structure.
Using an unadjusted peer beta can mis-state cost of equity, especially for highly leveraged firms.

lessons.example: Valuing a private company: take listed peers' betas, unlever them, then relever at the private company's D/E.

calc.problem: Unlevered beta 0.9; tax rate 25%; target D/E 0.5. Find the levered beta.

quiz.why: Financial risk adds to equity risk.

lessons.title: Adjusted present value (APV)
lessons.summary: Value the business and its financing effects separately.

term.meaning: Base-case NPV (all-equity) + PV of financing side effects (tax shields, subsidies, issue costs).

sections.b: APV = NPV if all-equity financed + PV(tax shields) − PV(issue costs) ± other financing effects. It is useful when capital structure changes over time, as in LBOs and project finance.
APV makes the value contributed by financing decisions transparent.

lessons.example: A project with a government-subsidised loan gets an APV boost from the interest subsidy.

calc.problem: All-equity NPV ₹50 crore; PV of interest tax shields ₹30 crore; debt issue costs ₹5 crore. Find APV.
steps: APV = Base NPV + PV tax shields − Issue costs

quiz.q: Debt issue costs in APV are…

lessons.title: Real options
lessons.summary: The value of flexibility in uncertain projects.

term.meaning: The right, but not obligation, to take a business action such as expanding, delaying or abandoning.

sections.b: Standard NPV ignores managerial flexibility. Strategic NPV = Static NPV + Option value. Common options: expand, delay, abandon, switch.
Pilot projects and phased investments often look unattractive on static NPV but are valuable because they create options.

lessons.example: A company launching in one city first keeps the option to expand nationally if demand proves strong, and to stop if not.

calc.problem: A pilot project has a static NPV of −₹20 crore, but the option to expand is valued at ₹35 crore. Find the strategic NPV.
steps: Strategic NPV = Static NPV + Option value

options: A right but not obligation to act
Option to expand a factory later

quiz.q: Static NPV may undervalue projects because it ignores…

lessons.title: Options: calls and puts
lessons.summary: Payoffs from the right to buy or sell.

term.meaning: The right to buy an asset at a fixed strike price before or at expiry.

sections.b: Call payoff = max(S − K, 0); put payoff = max(K − S, 0). Profit = payoff − premium paid. Buyers have limited loss (the premium); sellers take on larger risk. NSE has one of the world's highest volumes of index options.
Companies use options to hedge; investors use them to hedge or speculate. Understanding payoffs prevents costly mistakes.

lessons.example: SEBI studies have found that the large majority of individual traders in equity F&O lose money, a warning about speculative use.

calc.problem: You buy a call with strike ₹100 for a premium of ₹5. At expiry the stock is ₹120. Find the payoff and profit.

lessons.title: Put-call parity
lessons.summary: Calls, puts, stock and bonds are linked by arbitrage.

term.meaning: Risk-free profit from price differences; markets quickly eliminate it.

sections.b: For European options: C − P = S − K ÷ (1 + r)^T. If prices break this relationship, traders can lock in riskless profit, so prices stay in line.
Parity helps price options, detect mispricing and build synthetic positions.

lessons.example: A protective put (stock + put) has the same payoff as a call plus a bond, which is a synthetic equivalent.

calc.problem: Stock ₹100; strike ₹100; risk-free 5%; 1 year; call price ₹10. What should the put cost?

options: Calls, puts, stock and a bond
