lessons.title: Hedging with futures
lessons.summary: Lock in prices to protect margins.

term.meaning: A standardised exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a future date.

sections.b: A buyer worried about rising prices goes long futures; a producer worried about falling prices goes short. Gains on futures offset losses in the physical market and vice versa. Futures are marked to market daily.
Fuel, metals and agricultural price swings can wipe out margins; hedging stabilises earnings.

lessons.example: Airlines hedge jet fuel; jewellers hedge gold; sugar mills may hedge sugar prices.

calc.problem: An airline hedges 1,000 kilolitres of fuel at ₹90,000 per kL. The price rises to ₹1,00,000 per kL. How much did the hedge save?

quiz.q: A buyer fearing price rises should…
options: Buy puts on its own shares

lessons.title: Duration and bond price risk
lessons.summary: Measure how sensitive a bond is to rate changes.

term.meaning: Approximate % change in bond price for a 1% change in yield.

sections.b: % price change ≈ −Modified duration × Change in yield. Longer maturity and lower coupons → higher duration → more rate risk. Banks and insurers match asset and liability durations.
Duration is the main tool for managing interest-rate risk in bond portfolios and balance sheets.

lessons.example: Silicon Valley Bank's 2023 collapse was linked to holding long-duration bonds funded by short-term deposits as rates rose.

calc.problem: A bond priced at ₹1,000 has a modified duration of 5. Yields rise by 1%. Estimate the new price.

lessons.title: Value at Risk (VaR)
lessons.summary: How much could we lose on a bad day?

term.meaning: The maximum expected loss over a period at a given confidence level.

sections.b: Parametric VaR = Portfolio value × Volatility × z-score (1.65 for 95%, 2.33 for 99%). A 1-day 95% VaR of ₹25 lakh means losses should exceed ₹25 lakh on only about 1 day in 20.
Banks, treasuries and funds use VaR for risk limits and regulatory capital. But VaR doesn't say how bad the worst days can be (tail risk).

lessons.example: During market crashes, losses can far exceed VaR estimates, which is why stress testing complements it.

calc.problem: Portfolio ₹10 crore; daily volatility 1.5%; 95% confidence (z = 1.65). Find 1-day VaR.

options: Losses exceed ₹25 lakh about 1 day in 20

quiz.q: A key limitation of VaR is…
options: It ignores how bad tail losses can be

quiz.q: The z-score for 99% confidence is about…

lessons.title: Sharpe ratio
lessons.summary: Return per unit of risk.

term.meaning: (Portfolio return − Risk-free rate) ÷ Standard deviation of returns.

sections.b: Higher Sharpe means better risk-adjusted performance. It lets you compare funds or strategies with different risk levels.
Treasurers and investors shouldn't chase raw returns; they should compare returns per unit of risk.

lessons.example: Fund A returning 18% with high volatility may be worse than Fund B returning 14% with low volatility.

calc.problem: A portfolio returns 14%; risk-free rate 7%; standard deviation 20%. Find the Sharpe ratio.

quiz.why: Excess return per unit of risk.

quiz.q: The denominator of the Sharpe ratio is…

lessons.title: Free cash flow to equity (FCFE)
lessons.summary: Cash available to shareholders after debt holders.

term.meaning: FCFF − Interest × (1 − T) + Net borrowing.

sections.b: FCFE values equity directly when discounted at the cost of equity. It's useful for banks and companies with stable leverage.
FCFE shows how much could be paid as dividends or buybacks without hurting operations.

lessons.example: Analysts value banks with equity-based models because debt is part of their operations.

calc.problem: FCFF ₹275 crore; interest ₹40 crore; tax 25%; net new borrowing ₹20 crore. Find FCFE.

quiz.why: Borrowed cash is available to equity.

quiz.q: FCFE is often used to value…

lessons.title: Buybacks vs dividends
lessons.summary: Two ways to return cash, with different effects.

term.meaning: A company repurchasing its own shares, reducing shares outstanding.

sections.b: Buybacks reduce share count, raising EPS if earnings are unchanged. Dividends give cash to all shareholders. In theory both return value equally; in practice taxes, signalling and flexibility differ.
Capital return policy is a key board decision and a signal of management confidence.

lessons.example: Large Indian IT companies have used repeated buybacks alongside dividends to return surplus cash.

calc.problem: Net income ₹100 crore; shares 50 crore (EPS ₹2.00). The company buys back 10% of shares. Find the new EPS (assume net income unchanged).

quiz.q: A buyback usually ___ EPS if profit is unchanged.
Buybacks are often seen as a signal that management thinks shares are…
A benefit of buybacks vs regular dividends is…

lessons.title: Stock splits and bonus issues
lessons.summary: More shares, same company value.

term.meaning: Free additional shares to existing shareholders, funded from reserves.

sections.b: Splits divide each share into smaller units (e.g. ₹10 face value into ₹2). Bonus issues give extra shares (e.g. 1:1). Both raise share count and lower price proportionally; market cap and ownership % don't change.
They improve liquidity and affordability, but create no value by themselves.

lessons.example: Many Indian companies announce bonus issues after strong years, and share prices adjust on the ex-date.

calc.problem: 10 crore shares trade at ₹500. The company announces a 1:1 bonus. Find the new share count, theoretical price and market cap.
calc.answer: 20 crore shares at ≈ ₹250; market cap ₹5,000 crore

quiz.q: Does a stock split create value by itself?

lessons.title: IPOs and pre/post-money valuation
lessons.summary: How raising capital changes ownership.

term.meaning: Company value immediately after new investment = Pre-money + New money.

sections.b: Investor ownership = New money ÷ Post-money valuation. In an IPO, a fresh issue raises money for the company; an offer for sale (OFS) lets existing shareholders sell. SEBI regulates disclosures through the DRHP and RHP.
Understanding dilution and valuation is essential for founders, employees with ESOPs and investors.

lessons.example: Many Indian startup IPOs combine a fresh issue with an OFS by early investors.

calc.problem: Pre-money valuation ₹800 crore; a fresh issue raises ₹200 crore. Find post-money valuation and the new investors' stake.

quiz.q: In an offer for sale (OFS), money goes to…
The IPO draft document filed with SEBI is the…

lessons.title: Dilution across funding rounds
lessons.summary: How a founder's stake shrinks as the company grows.

term.meaning: Reduction in ownership percentage when new shares are issued.

sections.b: Each round, existing holders' stakes multiply by (1 − % sold in the round). ESOP pools also dilute. A smaller share of a much bigger company can still be worth far more.
Founders and employees must understand how much ownership they'll keep through seed, Series A, B and beyond.

lessons.example: Successful founders often end up with 10-25% at IPO, yet their stakes are worth hundreds or thousands of crores.

calc.problem: A founder owns 100%. Seed investors buy 20%; then Series A investors buy 25% of the post-round company. What does the founder own after Series A?

quiz.q: Why can dilution still be good?
options: A smaller share of a much bigger company can be worth more

lessons.title: Unit economics: LTV and CAC
lessons.summary: Does each customer make money over their lifetime?

term.meaning: Total sales and marketing spend ÷ new customers acquired.

sections.b: LTV (simplified) = ARPU × Gross margin ÷ Churn rate. LTV/CAC > 3 is a common benchmark; CAC payback = CAC ÷ (ARPU × Gross margin) in months.
Startups and digital businesses live or die by unit economics; growth with poor LTV/CAC burns cash.

lessons.example: Many quick-commerce and food-delivery businesses focus intensely on improving contribution per order and LTV/CAC.

calc.problem: ARPU ₹500 per month; gross margin 60%; monthly churn 5%; CAC ₹2,000. Find LTV, LTV/CAC and CAC payback.

quiz.q: A common healthy LTV/CAC benchmark is…

options: Sales and marketing spend to acquire customers

lessons.title: ESG and carbon pricing in decisions
lessons.summary: Putting a price on emissions changes project economics.

term.meaning: A notional cost per tonne of CO₂ that companies apply to projects to account for climate risk.

sections.b: ESG covers Environmental, Social and Governance factors. SEBI requires top listed companies to file a Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR). Internal carbon pricing makes future regulation and transition risks visible in NPV today.
Investors and lenders increasingly price ESG risks; green bonds and sustainability-linked loans offer financing advantages.

lessons.example: Several large Indian companies have adopted internal carbon prices and net-zero targets.

calc.problem: A project emits 10,000 tonnes of CO₂ per year. The company uses an internal carbon price of ₹2,000 per tonne. What annual cost is added to the project analysis?

quiz.q: SEBI's sustainability report for top listed companies is the…
An internal carbon price helps to…
options: Reflect climate risks in investment decisions

lessons.title: Capital allocation: the CEO's biggest job
lessons.summary: Where every rupee of capital goes decides long-term value.

term.meaning: Deciding how to deploy cash among reinvestment, acquisitions, debt reduction, dividends and buybacks.

sections.b: Options: reinvest in the business (if ROIC > WACC), acquire (if synergies > premium), pay down debt, pay dividends, buy back shares (if undervalued). The best allocators are disciplined and return cash when good opportunities are scarce.
Over a decade, capital allocation decisions often matter more to shareholder returns than operating performance.

lessons.example: William Thorndike's 'The Outsiders' profiles CEOs who created exceptional value mainly through disciplined capital allocation.
